mcqs.question: What mathematical properties must a CRDT's merge function have for it to guarantee strong eventual consistency?
options: It must be encrypted, compressed, and reversible
Commutative, associative, and idempotent — order, grouping, and duplicate application never change the result
It must run in constant time regardless of data size
It must always produce a smaller output than either input
mcqs.explanation: Commutativity, associativity, and idempotence together guarantee that any two replicas merging any sequence of updates, in any order, converge to the same state — that's the actual guarantee. Encryption, runtime complexity, and output size are unrelated to this property.

mcqs.question: Why does a PN-Counter need two separate G-Counters instead of one?
options: Two G-Counters are needed purely for redundancy in case one is lost
A single G-Counter cannot be replicated across more than one node
One G-Counter tracks increments and the other tracks decrements, since a G-Counter alone can only merge by taking a max and can't represent a value going down
PN-Counters don't actually use G-Counters internally
mcqs.explanation: A G-Counter's merge-by-max only works if values only ever grow; representing decrements requires a second, separate grow-only counter subtracted from the first. It isn't for redundancy, G-Counters do replicate across nodes, and PN-Counters are literally built from two G-Counters.

mcqs.question: In the PN-Counter code sample, why does merge() take the max of each replica's count instead of summing the two counters' values directly?
options: Taking the max is faster to compute than addition
Summing would cause an integer overflow on most systems
It's an arbitrary implementation choice with no effect on correctness
Summing directly would double-count updates a replica has already seen if the same state is merged more than once, breaking idempotence — max keeps the merge safe to repeat
mcqs.explanation: Using max per replica is exactly what makes re-merging the same state harmless (idempotent) — summing would double-count on a repeated or duplicate merge, violating the CRDT guarantee. It isn't about speed, overflow, or an arbitrary stylistic choice.

mcqs.question: What's a key practical advantage CRDTs have over operational transformation (OT) for collaborative editing?
options: CRDTs work naturally in a fully offline or peer-to-peer setting, without needing a central server to order operations
CRDTs are always simpler to implement than OT in every case
OT cannot be used for text editing at all
CRDTs guarantee zero network usage between replicas
mcqs.explanation: The real differentiator is coordination: CRDTs merge commutatively with no central broker required, which OT traditionally needs. CRDTs aren't universally simpler (the complexity shifts to designing the right data type), OT is exactly what Google Docs used for text, and CRDTs still need network communication to sync.

mcqs.question: A team uses an OR-Set CRDT to merge concurrent seat reservations, so two users reserving the same seat both end up in the merged "reserved" set. What went wrong?
options: Nothing — CRDTs always produce the mathematically correct outcome for any use case
The OR-Set's automatic "merge both" rule was applied to a case where the correct business answer required picking exactly one winner, not preserving both
OR-Sets cannot store reservation data of any kind
The bug is unrelated to using a CRDT — it would happen with any data structure
mcqs.explanation: This is exactly the CRDT pitfall: the data type's merge rule is fixed by its math, and "keep both" is wrong when the business rule requires a single winner, like one seat, one reservation. CRDTs don't guarantee business correctness for every use case, OR-Sets can technically store this data, and the bug is specific to using a merge-both structure for exclusive data.
